questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Integrals That Evaluate to Zero
questions.problem:
Which of the following integrals evaluates to zero due to symmetry?

- ${\int }_{-4}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-2}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-1}^{1}2\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to $0$ due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3(-x)) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3x) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) \\  & \ne -f(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The function $g(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)$ is an odd function, but integral II is not of the form ${\int }_{-a}^{a}g(x)\,\text{d}x$ since the upper and lower limits are not opposites. Therefore, we cannot use symmetry to simplify the integral.

- The function $h(x)=2\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}h(-x) & =2\operatorname{tan}⁡(-x) \\  & =-2\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\  & =-h(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}2\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Hence, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Integrals That Evaluate to Zero
questions.problem:
Which of the following integrals evaluates to zero due to symmetry?

- ${\int }_{-3}^{3}{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-2}^{2}x({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{x}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to zero due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x)={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4(-x)) \\  & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-4x) \\  & ={x}^{2}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)) \\  & =-{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x) \\  & =-f(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-3}^{3}{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

- The function $g(x)=x({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x})$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-x) & =(-x)({e}^{(-x)}+{e}^{-(-x)}) \\  & =-x({e}^{-x}+{e}^{x}) \\  & =-x({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}) \\  & =-g(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{2}x({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

- The function $h(x)={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}h(-x) & =(-x)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(-x)) \\  & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(-2x) \\  & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) \\  & \ne -h(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.knowledge_point: Simplifying Definite Integrals of Odd Functions
questions.problem: Given that ${\int }_{0}^{8}x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x=A,$ what is the value of ${\int }_{-8}^{0}x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{3})$ is an odd function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)\operatorname{cos}⁡((-x)^{3}) \\  & =(-x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(-{x}^{3}) \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{3}) \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{3})$ is an odd function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-8}^{8}x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Finally, using the adjacent intervals rule for integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-8}^{8}x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-8}^{0}x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{8}x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-8}^{0}x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x+A & =0 \\ {\int }_{-8}^{0}x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & =-A.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x),$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x).$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=x{e}^{{x}^{2}+1}$ is an odd function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x){e}^{(-x)^{2}+1} \\  & =-x{e}^{{x}^{2}+1} \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=x{e}^{{x}^{2}+1}$ is an odd function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-4}^{4}x{e}^{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Finally, using the adjacent intervals rule for integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{4}x{e}^{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-4}^{0}x{e}^{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{4}x{e}^{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-4}^{0}x{e}^{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x+p & =0 \\ {\int }_{-4}^{0}x{e}^{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x & =-p.\end{aligned}
$$
